The record:
Write the postmortem for the incident below.

Alert: HighErrorRate on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: Error rate above threshold for 5m {A1}
Alert raised: 2026-11-12T18:22:00Z {alert_raised}
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one. An alert rule fires; a person is paged. Argus first posted about the incident in Slack at 2026-11-12T18:22:02Z {first_told}, and the document says so already: leave that post out, and do not say that no person was told. That nobody was paged is a finding of its own.
The alert rule waits 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires. The alert came 6 minutes {detection_gap} after its series passed its line, within the 7 minutes 30 seconds {accounted_for} accounted for by its rule waiting 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute {rule_evaluated_every}, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds {scraping_allowance} for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute its series is read in.
Broken from 2026-11-12T18:15:00Z {began} (the onset, dated to its minute: a change came during that minute). The service was not back to normal by 2026-11-12T18:26:13Z {argus_stopped}, so it was broken for at least 11 minutes 13 seconds {duration} - a lower bound, not a measurement, and every impact figure below is bounded the same way.
Argus held the incident for 4 minutes 10 seconds {held}, until 2026-11-12T18:26:13Z {argus_stopped}. That is not how long the fault lasted, nor how long Argus went on working - leave it out of your answer.
The service's error rate over all its requests, before it began: 0.9% {errors_before}.
The same rate while it was broken: 30.5% {errors_while_broken}, peaking at 36.0% {errors_at_worst}.
Rise above baseline: 29.6% {errors_rise} of traffic failed that otherwise would not have.
The series behind the alert, `sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[1m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[1m]))` - its alert said "Error rate above threshold for 5m {A1}" - which its alert rule evaluates and calls worse rising: 0.9083333333333334% {series_before} before it began, 30.541666666666667% {series_while_broken} on average while it was broken, and 36% {series_at_worst} at its worst. Say what it measures in words, not by its query.
Customer loss: at least 7,545.67 USD {customer_loss} - how far the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier, beyond how much those hours vary on their own; a lower bound, counted with the service not seen back to normal.

Changes to production it read:

  - Deploys read, none came back.

Log lines it read, one per message:

Candidates it considered, in the Investigator's words - name them by their labels, but cite none; what they claim is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [C1, also C2] Candidates blaming the same move of monthly-spend-feature, each in its own words:
      C1: The feature flag monthly-spend-feature was switched on at 2026-11-12T18:15:47Z {C1.1}. Account page requests that evaluate it then fail with ZeroDivisionError at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47, and the error rate rose from about 1% {C1.2} to about 30% {C1.3}. No deployment or config change was recorded. [feature-flag-toggle, confidence 0.95 {C1.4}, refuted]
      C2: The feature flag monthly-spend-feature was switched on at 2026-11-12T18:15:47Z {C1.5}. Evaluations then moved from off to on, and account page requests started failing with a ZeroDivisionError at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47. The error rate went from about 1% {C1.6} to about 30% {C1.7}. No deployment is recorded, and the 3 {C1.8} replicas are converged. Latency, memory and CPU stayed flat. Argus switched the flag back off at 2026-11-12T18:22:13Z {C1.9}, but the logs still showed it on and errors continued through 18:25 {C1.10}. [feature-flag-toggle, confidence 0.88 {C1.11}, refuted, as tested for C1]

Actions it took:
  - [M1] Reverted the feature flag monthly-spend-feature for [C1] (can be put back) - refuted, put back when it did not help

What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] The fault is in `average_spend_per_item_this_month` in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. It divides `account.total_this_month_cents` by the number of purchases flagged `in_current_month`. When a shopper has bought nothing this month, that number is zero, and line 47 {F1.1} raises ZeroDivisionError. Plenty of shoppers have bought before but not this month (the test file's own helper calls this "the ordinary case"). So every request that `render_spend_summary` sent down the monthly path (`use_monthly_summary=True`) for such a shopper failed at the account-page boundary. Turning on monthly-spend-feature did not create the fault. It started sending requests to code that had always crashed on this input.
      
      The fix: when nothing was bought this month, the function now returns 0 {F1.2}, because a shopper with no purchases this month has spent 0 {F1.3} this month. For any month with at least one purchase it divides exactly as before. The lifetime figure (`average_spend_per_item`) is unchanged, so its existing test still expects ZeroDivisionError for an account that has never bought anything while the flag is off. The function's return type is still `int`, so `account_page._the_figure_for` and the rest of the page get the same kind of value as before.
      
      Tests added to tests/io_shop/test_spend_summary.py:
      - one calls `average_spend_per_item_this_month` directly, for a shopper with past purchases but none this month, and expects 0 {F1.4};
      - one goes through `render_spend_summary(..., use_monthly_summary=True)` and expects the same.
      
      With the code as it stood, both would raise ZeroDivisionError.
      
      Not addressed: the investigation reports the flag still evaluating "on" after it was switched off. Nothing I read in this repository evaluates or caches that flag (`rollout.py` holds only a share constant), so I made no change for it. With this fix, an "on" evaluation for such a shopper no longer fails.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'.

Action items the record already holds:
  - AI-1 (mitigate, open): Review and merge the proposed fix
PR #576 is a draft Argus opened for a person to review and merge. The record holds nothing about it after that: do not say it was reviewed, approved or merged, or that it was not - nor that the record holds nothing, which the document says itself. Nothing ran its test or its fix: say what it proposes, not that it corrects anything.

Cite evidence in causal_chain by its label. In a contributing factor's addressed_by, name the record's own action items that answer it, by their number; an item you propose names the factors it answers in its answers, by their labels.

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

The document, by field:
root_cause: The monthly path that monthly-spend-feature switches on works out a shopper's average spend per item this month by dividing the month's total by the number of purchases made this month. Nothing guards against that number being zero, so for every shopper who has bought before but not this month, line {F1.1} of src/io_shop/spend_summary.py raises ZeroDivisionError and the account page request fails. It rests on F1, a reading of the source nothing ran, so it is unverified.
cause_in_plain_words: An admin switched on a new feature that sent shoppers' account pages through a monthly spending calculation, and that calculation likely fails for anyone who has bought nothing so far this month.
still_at_risk: With monthly-spend-feature back on, account pages could keep failing for every shopper who has bought nothing this month, and switching the flag off in the flag provider might again not change what io-shop evaluates.
symptom: Shoppers' account pages failed
stops_the_harm: Switch monthly-spend-feature off again in a way that reaches every io-shop replica. Confirm at the service that io-shop's logs show the flag evaluating off, that the ZeroDivisionError lines from src/io_shop/spend_summary.py stop, and that the error rate falls back to about {errors_before}.
why_it_did_not_help: Find out why io-shop kept evaluating monthly-spend-feature as on after it was switched off in the flag provider at {P2.1}: whether the change reached the replicas at all, or was held back by caching, polling or another source of flag values. If it did reach them, find out why account pages kept failing.
causal_chain 1: Shoppers' account page requests failed with server errors, starting in the onset minute and continuing through the last minute read. (cites T5, under "What Argus did, in order"; Gbac1, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; G5309, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 2: The failing account page requests raised ZeroDivisionError in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. These errors appear in io-shop's logs from the onset minute onwards and not before it. (cites G5309, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 3: An admin switched the feature flag monthly-spend-feature on at {P1.1}. In that same minute, flag evaluations started moving from off to on, and from the next minute every evaluation came back on, which sent account page requests down the flag's monthly path. (cites P1, under "Changes to production it read"; G971b, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; Gce95, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 3 ruled_out 2: The revision running on every replica, which the history does not name. With it in place and the flag off, account pages rendered normally and the flag evaluated off in every minute read before the onset. (cites T33, under "What Argus did, in order"; Gad41, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; G7e5d, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 4: The monthly path likely divides by the number of purchases made this month, which is zero for shoppers who have bought nothing this month. (cites F1, under "What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix")
contributing_factors 1: No check was seen that exercised the monthly path behind monthly-spend-feature for a shopper with no purchases this month before the flag was switched on in production. By Code-Fix's reading, the tests in the file it read did not cover that case.
contributing_factors 1 had_it_been_otherwise: The division by zero would have been found before the flag was switched on, and account pages would not have failed.
contributing_factors 2: No staged rollout of the flag was seen. From the minute after it was switched on, every evaluation of monthly-spend-feature in io-shop came back on.
contributing_factors 2 had_it_been_otherwise: Only a small share of account page requests would have taken the failing path at first, and a halt on rising errors could have stopped it before it reached everyone.
contributing_factors 3: The HighErrorRate alert on io-shop paged nobody: no on-call incident was linked to it.
contributing_factors 3 had_it_been_otherwise: A person would have known about the failures as soon as the alert fired and could have stepped in when the automated revert did not take effect, shortening the incident.
contributing_factors 4: Switching monthly-spend-feature off in the flag provider did not change what io-shop evaluated: its logs kept showing the flag on after it was switched off.
contributing_factors 4 had_it_been_otherwise: Switching the flag off would have taken account pages off the failing path and ended the failures without waiting for a code fix.
action_items 1: Before a feature flag can be switched on in production, require tests that exercise the code path it enables, including edge cases such as a shopper with no purchases this month.
action_items 2: Roll out io-shop feature flags to a small share of requests first, and stop the rollout automatically when the error rate rises.
action_items 3: Link the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop to on-call paging so that a person is paged when it fires.
action_items 4: Alert when the flag state io-shop logs that it evaluates disagrees with the flag provider's state after a flag change.
went_wrong 1: C2 was marked refuted because of the test run for C1, even though C2 itself said that switching the flag off had not reached the service. The one action taken never got account pages off the monthly path, so it could not show whether the flag was the cause, and Argus moved on with no explanation left to try.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {T5.1} or {duration}, are figures code writes in from the row they name. They are not judged.
  - Action items propose what to do; they make no claim about the record.
  - Whether something went well, went wrong or was lucky is a judgement. Only a fact it states is judged, and whether a went_wrong item is one its field excludes.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.
